analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Dodd-Frank process for winding down failing giant financial companies.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the repeal on a 34-22 vote in May 2016, but the full House never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Title II of the Dodd-Frank law gives the government a special process, run by the FDIC, to take apart a failing giant bank or financial company in an orderly way, paid for by fees on the biggest financial firms. This bill would delete that process entirely and send failing giants back through ordinary bankruptcy court instead. It cleared the House Financial Services Committee but was never brought to the House floor for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest banks and other big financial companies gain, because they would no longer be subject to the orderly liquidation regime, the wind-down planning requirements that come with it, or the industry-funded mechanism for resolving a failing giant. Creditors of failed firms could also fare better, since bankruptcy lets them negotiate claims directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The largest banks and financial firms

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Title II of Dodd-Frank, removing the FDIC's authority to resolve failing systemically important financial companies outside of bankruptcy [S2][S4].
It strikes the conforming provisions in the Federal Deposit Insurance Act and Federal Reserve Act that supported the orderly liquidation process, so no replacement regime is created [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the risk. If a firm the size of Lehman Brothers fails under ordinary bankruptcy, the fallout can freeze credit markets, cost jobs, and — as in 2008 — generate pressure for taxpayer-funded rescues. Supporters counter that ordinary bankruptcy treats all firms the same and ends a regime they saw as enshrining bailouts of big firms' creditors.

drawbacks.text: Removing orderly liquidation authority means a failing giant financial company goes through Chapter 11 bankruptcy, a process designed for ordinary companies; a disorderly failure of a systemically important firm can spread losses across the economy, which is the problem Title II was written to solve after Lehman Brothers' chaotic 2008 collapse [S2].

Supporters' strongest argument is that Title II gave the executive branch discretion to determine which companies get the special resolution process, potentially shielding some firms and their creditors from market discipline; ordinary bankruptcy applies the same rules to everyone.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that repeal eliminates the industry-funded wind-down mechanism and leaves no dedicated process for a failing giant, gambling that bankruptcy courts can handle a firm whose failure threatens the whole financial system [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill benefits a narrow set of very large financial institutions, whose main gains are escaping a resolution regime designed for them and the fees and planning burdens that come with it. The cost, if the regime was ever needed, falls broadly on the public through the risk of a disorderly failure and potential rescues. The bill offers no replacement mechanism, so the trade-off is entirely about which failure process the country would rather have.

outcome.mechanism: The Financial Services Committee approved it and it sat on the House calendar, but the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 11, 2016 and referred to four committees: Financial Services, Agriculture, Judiciary, and Ways and Means [S1][S6].
The Financial Services Committee ordered it reported on a 34-22 vote on April 13, 2016 [S6].
The committee reported the bill on May 19, 2016; the other three committees were discharged, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 444) [S3][S6].
The bill never received a vote by the full House, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, killing the bill [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's existing protections stayed on the books, because the repeal never reached a vote. Large financial institutions keep bearing the Dodd-Frank resolution regime they sought to escape, so nobody gained what the bill would have delivered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firms still under Dodd-Frank's resolution rules

industries.industry: Large banks and systemically important financial institutions
industries.note: Repeal would free the biggest financial firms from the orderly liquidation regime, its resolution-planning requirements, and the industry-funded wind-down mechanism. The benefit is private; the added failure risk falls on the broader economy.

Under Title II, the FDIC could impose losses on a failing firm's creditors; ordinary bankruptcy gives creditors standard claims and negotiating power. This shifts resolution economics back toward creditor recovery.
The bill strips the FDIC of its authority to take over and dismantle failing nonbank financial companies, eliminating the tool it was given after 2008 to avoid taxpayer rescues.
